extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples for reporting investigations, legislation, and meetings — showing different treatments (full, condensed, abridged) and techniques for municipal, institutional, and human-interest stories. The page provides model copy illustrating how to structure leads, use quotes, follow up on prior reports, and employ descriptive detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of news writing — investigations, legislation, and meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Section heading: 'INVESTIGATIONS, LEGISLATION, AND MEETINGS' (appears as the topical grouping for the sample items).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page groups sample items under the topical category to illustrate how to cover official hearings, municipal legislation, public meetings, conventions, and organized inquiries — showing both straight reporting and human-interest approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label and indicate editing status of item
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories begin with source attribution and edit-status markers, e.g., '(Condensed)', '(Abridged)' and the newspaper name such as 'Philadelphia Ledger (Condensed)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always credit the source newspaper and, when publishing an edited or shortened version, indicate that it is 'condensed' or 'abridged' so readers know the item is an edited reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up-story linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit note in text: 'Note — The second of the next two stories follows up the news of the introduction of an ordinance given in the first story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting a pair (or series) of items, clearly indicate the relationship between them: identify which piece introduces the action and which one is a follow-up reporting developments or reactions to that initial item.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard-news lead for municipal/legislative items
rubrics_metrics.description: Example lead: 'Authority for the immediate erection of a two-track elevated railway from Front and Arch streets to Rhawn street, Holmesburg, is granted in an ordinance introduced in Common Council yesterday by Peter E. Costello, of the 45th Ward.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For municipal/legislative stories open with the central authoritative action: who enacted or introduced the measure, what the measure does, where it applies, and when; include critical operational details (routes, timelines, franchise terms, fares, approvals) so readers immediately grasp the public import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of direct quotation and reported speech to show participants' voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous verbatim quotes are used to convey reactions and local color (e.g., 'Don’t you do it; you’ll be fined,' 'You see a lot of drunken men coming out of saloons, but you never see a drunken chicken coming out of a chicken coop.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed exact quotations from stakeholders, officials, and attendees to capture emotion, opposition, and humor; use these quotes to illustrate community response and to lend credibility and immediacy to the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene-setting and anecdotal human-interest detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include detailed descriptive passages (e.g., the Social Workers’ Club 'born about five years ago...a healthy infant at first' and Friends' Meeting 'soft stillness...the great, square-paned windows').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For human-interest or meeting-feature pieces, open or work in vivid scene-setting and short anecdotes that convey mood and personalities; sensory detail and gentle narrative make reports more engaging for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rhetorical devices (questions, contrasts) to engage readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Example device: ending the 'women ushers' item with a rhetorical question and contrast — 'Meanwhile—who are braver, girls or boys? ... And you—?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ well-placed rhetorical questions, contrasts, or short summative lines to prompt reader reflection or to provide a memorable close, particularly in feature or argumentative items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present multiple angles / opposing viewpoints in civic reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples show managers, city officials, aldermen, and citizens giving differing perspectives on the same issue (e.g., Director Taylor vs. Councilman Costello; proponents vs. opponents of the Justice of the Peace bill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering legislation or public policy, present the main competing positions, name proponents and opponents, and report their principal arguments and motives (including political implications), so readers understand the stakes and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include operational and technical specifics when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: City-council item lists concrete technical and contractual details: route descriptions, station stops, construction timelines, fare limits, overhead clearance, franchise sharing and profit terms (10% of net profits), and approval procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete operational facts (routes, stations, clearances, fares, timelines, financial terms, approval steps) in legislative or infrastructure reporting — these specifics are essential for public understanding and for assessing impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use irony and character sketches to humanize routine reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Items such as the Old Clothes Dealers' meeting and the Social Workers’ Club obituary use ironic humor and character sketches ('The Social Workers’ Club is dead...the end came peacefully') to enliven coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where appropriate, apply light irony, caricature, or brief character portraits to make otherwise routine organizational news more readable while remaining accurate and fair to subjects.
